sections.h2: What does selling in Ocean Township, NJ involve?
sections.html:
Ocean Township occupies east central Monmouth County, and no buyer may move into a house there until the Housing Division has issued a Code Compliance Inspection Certificate. The requirement follows the property, so it applies to an agent listing, a private sale and a cash purchase alike.

Federal estimates put the population at 28,088 spread across 10.87 square miles of land, up from 27,672 in the 2020 count. This page covers the Monmouth County township, which is a different place from Ocean Township in Ocean County. There is no central downtown. Homes cluster in three communities, Oakhurst, Wanamassa and Wayside, so people usually describe a house by its neighborhood.

The township has used the council-manager form under New Jersey's Faulkner Act since July 1, 1963. A five-member council sets policy, and an appointed manager runs daily administration, so permit and inspection questions go to staff offices rather than to elected officials.

sections.h2: Where do Oakhurst, Wanamassa and Wayside sit within Ocean Township?
sections.html:
State lawmakers formed the township on February 21, 1849 out of Shrewsbury Township, and over the following decades Long Branch, Asbury Park, Deal, Allenhurst and other shore towns were cut away. The remainder touches Eatontown and West Long Branch on the north, Long Branch, Deal, Allenhurst and Interlaken on the east, Neptune and Asbury Park on the south and Tinton Falls on the west.

ZIP code 07755 covers Oakhurst, and 07712 covers Wanamassa and Wayside. Deal Lake, 158 acres shared among seven municipalities along roughly 27 miles of shoreline, touches the township and has been under the Deal Lake Commission since 1974. A house near the water should be ready for questions about basement moisture, which is also something the inspector checks.

sections.h2: What are Ocean Township homes worth, and who lives in them?
sections.html:
A typical owned home carries a $678,300 value in the 2020 to 2024 figures, and 62.7 percent of households own their place. More than one in five residents is 65 or older, and over 90 percent stayed put last year, so many houses change hands rarely and may be due for updates.

sections.h2: What does the Ocean Township Housing Division inspect?
sections.html:
The Housing Division covers every sale and every rental that changes hands. Its forms page says sale permits must be closed before you call for the visit, post-dated checks are sent back and the office keeps weekday hours from 8:30 to 4:30. The checklist is a visual look at:

  • The outside: flaking paint, gutters and leaders, doors, windows, screens, siding, sheds, fences, trash and weeds.
  • A street number at least 3 inches tall that can be read from the road.
  • A handrail once stairs pass four risers, and a guardrail on any open porch or landing above 30 inches.
  • The inside: kitchen and bath plumbing, walls and ceilings, leaks or cellar water, outlets with covers, locks and ventilation.
  • A water heater fitted with a pressure and temperature valve and extension pipe.
  • An anti-tip bracket for stoves manufactured after 1991.

Before the visit, line up three things:

  • Close every open permit.
  • Keep gas, electric and water running on inspection day.
  • Gather a lab report if the house has its own well.

A private well needs a certified lab report that meets state environmental standards. The forms page also offers a lead paint information sheet.

sections.h2: Which fire district handles the smoke and carbon monoxide forms?
sections.html:
Those forms are separate from the Housing Division visit. Ocean Township has Fire District No. 1 and No. 2, and the township's forms page links an online smoke detector, carbon monoxide and extinguisher application for both. Ask the district covering your street which one applies.

State rules also demand a smoke alarm compliance certificate, issued through the municipality, for a house with one or two units. It stays valid for six months, so schedule the fire visit so it still covers your closing date.

sections.h2: Which state fees and deadlines touch an Ocean Township sale?
sections.html:
Recording the deed triggers the seller's Realty Transfer Fee, and the Division of Taxation's schedule shows lower rates for qualifying senior, blind or disabled sellers. The buyer's extra 1 percent starts above $1,000,000, a level that most local sales will not reach with a median near $678,300.

The seller also signs a GIT/REP form that goes to the county with the deed.

Monmouth County runs a calendar of its own for assessment appeals. According to the state's Form A-1, the Monmouth County Tax Board must receive a petition by January 15, or 45 days after notices are mailed if that is later, and a petition that arrives after the close of business that day is dismissed.

sections.h2: How do Route 18, the shore trains and the schools affect Ocean Township buyers?
sections.html:
Route 18 runs through the western side and Route 35 through the east. Route 66 marks the southern edge with Neptune, and Route 71 follows the eastern boundary beside Deal, West Long Branch and Long Branch. The Garden State Parkway lies just west, in Tinton Falls. Of its roughly 132 miles of road, about 120 belong to the township. Retail gathers along the main routes, with Ocean Commons on Route 35 and Seaview Shopping Center off Route 66.

A brief piece of the North Jersey Coast Line crosses the east side, though the nearest stops are Allenhurst and Elberon. NJ Transit buses 832 and 837 serve the township, and the SeaStreak ferry terminal in Highlands is a 25 to 30 minute drive.

The Ocean Township School District ran five schools and enrolled 3,263 students in 2023-24: elementary schools in Oakhurst, Wanamassa and Wayside, an intermediate school for grades 5 to 8 and the high school in Oakhurst. Expect buyers to ask which elementary school serves a given address. Joe Palaia Park, the township's largest, hosts the July 4 event and has a disc golf course, and the township also runs a membership pool and tennis club that is open from Memorial Day to Labor Day.

sections.h2: When should an Ocean Township owner consider a cash offer?
sections.html:
A cash price deserves a look when the house would struggle with the checklist and repairs are unwelcome, when it came to you through an estate, or when a firm closing date matters. Have the buyer put in writing who orders the Housing Division visit and who covers corrections.

Landlords should note that the township requires rental registration and payment before March 1. If a tenant-occupied house is being sold, agree with the tenant and buyer how the change of occupancy will be handled.

faqs.q: Must an Ocean Township house be inspected before it changes hands?
faqs.a: Yes. The Housing Division performs the code compliance inspection on sales and on rentals with a new occupant. Open sale permits have to be closed first, and nobody may move in before the certificate exists.

faqs.q: What is on the Ocean Township checklist?
faqs.a: A visual review inside and out: paint, gutters, a 3-inch street number, handrails beyond four risers, plumbing, leaks, outlet covers, the water heater valve and extension pipe, and an anti-tip bracket on newer stoves.

faqs.q: What is the Monmouth County assessment appeal date?
faqs.a: January 15, unless notices were mailed late enough to extend it. The state form names Monmouth, Burlington and Gloucester as the counties with this earlier date, while other counties keep April 1.

faqs.q: How long does an Ocean Township smoke alarm certificate last?
faqs.a: Six months. The certificate comes through the municipality, and in Ocean Township the fire districts supply the application forms.

faqs.q: Does the seller pay the extra 1 percent state fee?
faqs.a: No, the buyer does, and only above $1,000,000. A seller pays the regular Realty Transfer Fee, which follows the price in the deed and any exemption claimed.
